claim: Conditional expression of genes and observation of phenotype remain central to biological discovery.

claim: Current methods enable either on/off or imprecisely controlled graded gene expression.

claim: WTC846 enables precisely adjustable, graded, growth condition independent expression of genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

claim: Temperature-sensitive mutations have been used to give insight into ordinality of cell biological events.

claim: In 2021, contemporaneous approaches to conditional expression include construction of transgenes activated by chimeric activators controlled by promoters whose expression is temporally and spatially restricted to different cell lineages.

source: For example, controlled expression of the bacteriophage λ cI and cro gene products was key to understanding how changes in the level of those proteins regulated the phage's decision to undergo lytic or lysogenic growth (Maurer et al., 1980; Meyer et al., 1980; Meyer and Ptashne, 1980).

claim: In S. cerevisiae, contemporaneous means to tune dosage include metabolite induced promoters, such as PGAL1, PMET3, PCUP1.

claim: Many inducible systems depend on fusions between eukaryotic and viral activator domains and prokaryotic proteins.
source: Many of these depend on fusions between eukaryotic and viral activator domains and prokaryotic proteins (Garí et al., 1997; Ottoz et al., 2014; McIsaac et al., 2013; McIsaac et al., 2014) that bind sites on engineered promoters (Brent and Ptashne, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Current inducible systems suffer from basal expression when not induced.
source: These methods suffer from a number of drawbacks, including basal expression when not induced (Bellí et al., 1998; Garí et al., 1997; Ottoz et al., 2014)

claim: Current inducible systems have deleterious effects on cell growth due to sequestration of cellular components by the activation domain.
source: deleterious effects on cell growth due to sequestration of cellular components by the activation domain (Gill and Ptashne, 1988)

claim: Current inducible systems cause induction of genes in addition to the controlled gene.

claim: Inducible systems rely on 'activation by recruitment'.

claim: In activation by recruitment, the activator binds a site on DNA upstream of a yeast gene and recruits general transcription factors and regulators of the Pre-Initiation Complex.
source: the activator binds a site on DNA upstream of a yeast gene and recruits general transcription factors and regulators of the Pre-Initiation Complex (PIC).

claim: General transcription factors and regulators of the PIC assemble downstream at the 'core promoter' and recruit RNA polymerase II to induce transcription.
source: These assemble downstream at the 'core promoter' and recruit RNA polymerase II to induce transcription (Hahn and Young, 2011).

claim: An alternative to inducible activation would be to engineer reversible repression of yeast transcription by prokaryotic repressors.
source: An alternative to inducible activation would be to engineer reversible repression of yeast transcription by prokaryotic repressors (Brent and Ptashne, 1984; Hu and Davidson, 1987; Brown et al., 1987).

claim: For TATA-containing promoters, binding of prokaryotic proteins such as LexA and the lac repressor near the TATA sequence can repress transcription.

source: presumably by interference with the formation of the PIC, transcription initiation, or early elongation.

claim: Prokaryotic repressors likely work through different mechanisms than mechanisms used by repressors native to eukaryotes.
source: It has long been recognized (Brent, 1985) that prokaryotic repressors likely work through different mechanisms than mechanisms used by repressors native to eukaryotes (Wang et al., 2011; Gaston and Jayaraman, 2003).
